question:
Patient note:
A 48-year-old man arrived to the combined pulmonary–rheumatology follow-up clinic this morning at the request of his occupational medicine physician for a comprehensive status review before he returns to his seasonal post as a helicopter mechanic for a forestry service. Seven years ago he began experiencing progressive exertional shortness of breath and a daily morning cough productive of scant white sputum; spirometry at that time demonstrated an FEV1/FVC ratio of 58 % with only a 4 % rise after bronchodilator, and high-resolution CT revealed centrilobular emphysematous changes confined to the upper lobes. Since then he has used a long-acting muscarinic antagonist inhaler every morning, a combination inhaled corticosteroid–long-acting beta agonist twice daily, and albuterol as needed—typically three rescue puffs per week. He reports no episodes of respiratory failure, nocturnal ventilation, or hospital admissions for flare-ups, though he was treated with a five-day prednisone burst last winter during an influenza infection. He smoked a pack a day from age 18 to 40 and stopped after his youngest child was born; he denies marijuana or vaping exposure. In addition, he carries a diagnosis of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis first recognized five years ago when he developed symmetrical swelling and morning stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal joints; radiographs already showed marginal erosions of the second and third MCPs. He self-administers methotrexate 20 mg subcutaneously each week and takes hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, with good control of joint pain and no extra-articular nodules, vasculitis, or ocular inflammation. He performs overhead mechanical tasks for several hours at a stretch without difficulty but notes occasional grip weakness after prolonged work. Three years ago, during a routine wellness examination, fasting plasma glucose was 129 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 6.4 %; subsequent dietary counseling plus a structured exercise program led to weight loss of 8 kg, and his most recent A1c checked last month was 6.2 % without pharmacologic therapy. He denies visual blurring, paresthesias, foot ulcers, or laboratory evidence of albuminuria on serial urine micro-albumin screens. Eighteen months ago an incidental 2.1-cm enhancing mass in the lower pole of the left kidney was detected on abdominal ultrasound performed for nonspecific flank discomfort. He underwent laparoscopic partial nephrectomy with negative margins; surgical pathology confirmed a clear-cell carcinoma confined to the renal cortex without vascular invasion. Surveillance CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis performed six weeks ago did not identify nodal enlargement, pulmonary nodules, or skeletal lesions, and serum creatinine afterward stabilized at 0.9 mg/dL. He has never experienced crushing retrosternal pain, diaphoresis, palpitations, exertional angina, lower-extremity edema responsive to diuretics, or orthopnea, and an echocardiogram ordered two years ago for an incidental systolic murmur revealed normal left-ventricular dimensions and an ejection fraction of 64 % without wall-motion abnormalities. He likewise denies transient speech difficulty, facial droop, limb weakness, seizures, or radiologic evidence of cerebral infarction. He consumes two beers on weekends, abstains from illicit substances, and his father died at 73 from complications of chronic liver cirrhosis attributed to hepatitis C, while his mother, now 75, lives independently with osteoarthritis; there is no family history of early myocardial infarction, stroke, or connective-tissue disorders. Current medications include the inhalers noted above, methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, folic acid 1 mg daily, over-the-counter fish oil, and ibuprofen as needed for joint flares; he uses no systemic corticosteroids chronically and no nephrotoxic analgesics. Vital signs today show temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 78 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 95 % on ambient air, and body mass index 26 kg/m². He appears well muscled, in no distress, and converses easily without breaks for breath. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs, and jugular venous pulsation is not elevated. Lungs demonstrate scattered end-expiratory wheezes with good air entry bilaterally and no crackles. The abdomen is soft and nontender with a well-healed 4-cm laparoscopic scar in the left flank; liver edge is not palpable, and there is no splenomegaly or ascites. Hands show mild ulnar deviation at the second and third MCPs, minimal synovial thickening, and full passive range of motion; grip strength is 4/5 bilaterally. Distal pulses are 2+ and symmetric; there is no lower-extremity edema or trophic skin change. Neurologic screening reveals intact cranial nerves, full strength proximally and distally, normal sensation, and a steady tandem gait. Laboratory studies drawn this morning display hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.2 × 10⁹/L (with an absolute neutrophil count of 3.8 × 10⁹/L), platelets 235 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 96 mL/min/1.73 m²), AST 22 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 4.5 g/dL, international normalized ratio 1.0, fasting glucose 118 mg/dL, and lipid profile with LDL 82 mg/dL and HDL 46 mg/dL. Spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 18 mg/g. A 12-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min, normal intervals, and no Q waves or ST-T changes. Post-bronchodilator spirometry repeated today is unchanged from prior baseline with FEV1 52 % predicted and FEV1/FVC 0.56. Hand radiographs obtained for comparison illustrate stable mild joint space narrowing without new erosions. He seeks confirmation that his airway, joint, glycemic, and oncologic conditions remain stable enough to permit physically demanding fieldwork and requests guidance on optimizing vaccination and lung health during the forthcoming wildfire season.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index sums weighted comorbidities; the age adjustment begins at 50 years. Based on the conditions present at this visit:
- Age 48: 0 points.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: emphysema with persistent airflow obstruction (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.56): 1 point.
- Connective tissue disease: seropositive rheumatoid arthritis: 1 point.
- Solid tumor without metastases diagnosed within 5 years: localized renal cell carcinoma resected 18 months ago, with no metastases on surveillance: 2 points.
- Glycemic abnormality managed by diet and exercise alone, without medication or end-organ damage: 0 diabetes points.
- No moderate-to-severe renal disease (eGFR 96) or other qualifying comorbidity: 0 points.
Total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 0 = 4.
Final answer: 4
